passage:
Week one. Preeti sent the weekly report two hours late again. Ayesha smiled in the meeting. “No problem.” Her jaw was tight under the smile.

Week three. Preeti reused Ayesha's slides without asking. Ayesha smiled. “Fine, whatever works.” Afterwards she typed a message to Preeti, deleted it, and typed a lighter one about lunch.

Week five. Preeti asked in front of the team, “Can someone lend me a pen?” and Ayesha snapped, “You never bring anything! Not a pen, not a report on time, not a thank-you!” The room froze. Preeti stared. Ayesha's hands shook. “It's not about the pen,” she said, too late.

qa.q: What did Preeti ask for in front of the team?
qa.a: Preeti asked whether someone could lend a pen.

qa.q: Why did Ayesha snap over a pen?
qa.a: Ayesha had held back irritation for weeks, so a small trigger let all the unspoken frustration out.

qa.q: What could Ayesha have done in week one or week three?
qa.a: Ayesha could have told Preeti privately and calmly about the late reports and the reused slides.

qa.q: What might Preeti have felt hearing the outburst without warning?
qa.a: Preeti probably felt shocked and confused, since Ayesha had smiled for weeks and never named a problem.

grounding: A team member holds back irritation for weeks, smiling in meetings, until a small trigger produces an outburst.

passage:
Madhav, sit. You keep saying “it's fine” about your project partner, and I remember saying the same. I'm Payal. At twenty-four I shared a small flat with Gaurav. He played music past midnight, finished my milk and left his wet towel on my chair. I smiled at all of it for two months and said “no problem.” Then one cold morning, before an important exam, I found the hot water gone again. I stood outside the bathroom and yelled, “Every single day! You never think of anyone!” Our neighbour opened her door to look. Gaurav came out dripping and stared at me. “Why didn't you ever say?” he asked quietly.

I had no answer. We stayed polite until the lease ended, but we never cooked together again. It would have taken one calm sentence in the first week.

qa.q: What did Payal find on the cold morning before the exam?
qa.a: Payal found the hot water gone again.

qa.q: Why did Payal yell over the hot water?
qa.a: Payal had smiled through two months of irritation and felt worn down and frustrated, so the hot water set off all the stored-up anger at once.

qa.q: Which choice in the first weeks could have changed how things went between Payal and Gaurav?
qa.a: Payal could have told Gaurav calmly about the music, the milk or the towel early on, instead of saying “no problem” for two months.

qa.q: How might Gaurav have felt coming out of the bathroom to the yelling?
qa.a: Gaurav probably felt shocked and confused, since Payal had said “no problem” for two months, which is why Gaurav asked why Payal had never said anything.

grounding: An elder recalls smiling through a flatmate's habits for two months until a small trigger set off an outburst that the household never quite recovered from.

passage:
For two months, at the rural bank branch in Sehore, Himani had watched Bidisha leave early every Friday. Himani stayed to close the cash. She said nothing. When Bidisha said, “Thanks, yaar, you're the best,” Himani smiled.
She smiled in meetings. She smiled when the manager praised Bidisha's customer numbers. She smiled when Bidisha borrowed her calculator and didn't return it.
Then one Friday, Bidisha picked up Himani's pen from her desk.
“That's MY PEN!” Himani shouted, so loudly that a farmer in the queue jumped. “And my calculator! And my Fridays!”
The branch went silent. Bidisha stared at her. Himani's face burned. She hadn't known how much had been piling up until it came out all at once.

qa.q: What did Bidisha pick up from Himani's desk?
qa.a: She picked up Himani's pen.

qa.q: Why did Himani shout over a pen?
qa.a: She had held back resentment and anger for two months behind smiles, so a small trigger released all of it.

qa.q: What could Himani do to stop this happening again?
qa.a: She could raise small issues early and calmly, like the Fridays and the calculator, before they build up.

qa.q: How might Bidisha have felt when Himani shouted?
qa.a: Bidisha was probably shocked and confused, not knowing Himani had been upset for weeks.

grounding: Shows a young bank clerk holding back irritation for weeks with smiles, until a small trigger produces an outburst.

passage:
In every meeting at the Lisbon design office, Ulla interrupted Paulo. Paulo would start explaining a layout, and Ulla would say, “Let me just add—” and take over.
For six weeks, Paulo smiled and said, “Of course, go ahead.” At home he told his flatmate he didn't mind.
Then on Thursday, in the kitchen, Ulla finished the coffee and didn't make more. Paulo stared at the empty pot.
“You never make more!” he shouted. “And you never let me finish a single sentence in meetings!”
Ulla froze with her cup halfway up.
Two colleagues at the table looked away. Paulo stood there, heart racing, realising he'd been angry for weeks. Over coffee.

qa.q: What did Ulla fail to do in the kitchen?
qa.a: She finished the coffee and didn't make more.

qa.q: Why did Paulo explode over an empty coffee pot?
qa.a: He had held back irritation and anger for six weeks while smiling, so a small trigger released it all at once.

qa.q: What went wrong in how Paulo handled the interruptions?
qa.a: He hid his feelings and told himself he didn't mind; speaking to Ulla calmly in week one would have prevented the outburst.

qa.q: How might Ulla have felt when Paulo shouted?
qa.a: She was likely shocked and embarrassed, freezing with her cup halfway up.

grounding: Shows a young professional who smiles through weeks of irritation until a small trigger produces an outburst.

passage:
For six weeks Sumit smiled through it. On every client call Karthik took the last slot to "add a quick point", which was always Sumit's point, said louder. Sumit said nothing. It wasn't worth a scene, he told himself. At home he complained to his flatmate; at work he typed "Sure, no problem!" in the chat.
On Thursday, in the small meeting room with Anjali and the new intern, Karthik reached over and moved Sumit's coffee mug off the laptop charger. That was all.
Sumit stood up so fast his chair hit the wall. "Can you stop touching my things and stop taking my work? Every single call!"
The intern froze. Anjali stared at the table.
Karthik blinked. "I... didn't know you felt that way."
Sumit sat down, face hot, hands shaking. The mug was not the problem. It never had been.

qa.q: What did Karthik move off the laptop charger?
qa.a: Sumit's coffee mug.

qa.q: What was Sumit feeling during the six weeks of smiling?
qa.a: Sumit felt growing irritation and resentment, hidden behind "Sure, no problem!" in the chat.

qa.q: What could Sumit have done in the first week?
qa.a: Tell Karthik privately and calmly that repeating his points on calls bothered him, before the anger built up.

qa.q: What was the outburst like for the intern?
qa.a: The intern froze, probably shocked and uncomfortable at a sudden blow-up with no idea of its history.

grounding: Shows a team member hiding irritation for weeks behind smiles until a tiny trigger sets off an outburst.
